Female Pacific sanddab reach an ultimate total length of 41 centimeters [Li = 41 centimeters], a size substantially larger than that of males, reflecting the pronounced sexual size dimorphism common among pleuronectiform flatfishes. This maximum recorded length was derived from extensive trawl surveys conducted off the central California coast, where individuals exceeding 40 centimeters are encountered infrequently. The species is a commercially important bycatch component of the groundfish fishery, and its life-history parameters have been estimated from decades of stock-assessment sampling.

Sexual maturation in female Pacific sanddab begins when individuals attain a total length at puberty of 11.9 centimeters [Lp = 11.9 centimeters]. This relatively modest size at the onset of gonadal development permits early reproductive participation, a strategy consistent with the moderately fast life-history pace of this species. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from field-collected specimens confirms that vitellogenesis initiates at this length, marking the transition to reproductive capability.

Eggs of the Pacific sanddab are spherical, pelagic, and possess a single oil globule, with a diameter typically ranging from 0.7 to 0.8 millimeters. From this oocyte diameter, and assuming a density slightly above that of seawater, the wet weight at birth for a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is estimated at 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams]. This extremely small initial mass reflects the lecithotrophic strategy of the prolarval stage, during which the developing larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for nutrition prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. The small size at hatch also renders the early larvae highly vulnerable to planktonic predators.

As female Pacific sanddab continue to grow and approach their asymptotic size, the corresponding maximum adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, reaches approximately 873 grams [Wwi = approximately 873 grams]. This value is derived from a length-weight relationship fitted to data from over two thousand specimens collected during NOAA fisheries surveys. By contrast, at the length marking the onset of puberty, the wet weight at puberty is considerably smaller, estimated at 19.6 grams [Wwp = 19.6 grams]. The nearly forty-five-fold increase in mass between puberty and the ultimate size underscores the substantial somatic growth that Pacific sanddab undergo after first becoming reproductively active.

Longevity data for Pacific sanddab, collected from otolith age-readings of individuals captured in the Southern California Bight, indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild approaches 9 years [am = 9 years] when assessed under the prevailing oceanographic conditions at a temperature of 10.3 °C [T = 10.3 °C]. This lifespan estimate, corresponding to an average bottom temperature of 10.3 °C [T = 10.3 °C], places the species among the moderately long-lived members of the genus Citharichthys. Individuals inhabiting cooler, deeper waters along the continental slope may exhibit slightly slower growth and consequently greater ages, though otolith-based validation of such extreme-age individuals remains limited.
